paras: The Savannah railroad bridge clash was a confrontation on the morning of September 22, 1881, in Savannah, Georgia, in which police charged a crowd of Black strikers who had rushed a train bringing replacement laborers. Five Black men were wounded, none seriously according to the wire report, and one of them, Wm. Williams, was shot in the leg. The clash drew notice because a dispatch carried in Northern papers reported eight men killed, a figure the Savannah and wire accounts do not support.

The strike began on Monday, September 19, when Black laborers loading the steamship Gate City demanded $2 a day and quit work when refused. That day a man in a crowd of strikers shot a mounted police sergeant named Harvey, and the employers hired new hands who loaded the ships under police protection.

In a petition dated September 22, the strikers said they had earned $1.25, $1.50 and $2.00 a day the year before and asked for $2.00, $2.50 and $3.00, citing higher prices for groceries, meat and rent.

According to the wire report, a morning train brought 150 laborers into the city, and the strikers gathered at the bridge and "made a rush for the train with the intention of driving off the hands." The police ordered them back and, "meeting with resistance," charged into the crowd, in the Richmond copy "with assistance." Five "negroes" were wounded and the rest scattered "in every direction."

The Savannah Morning News headlined the episode "A Conflict on the Railroad Bridge- Several Wounded" and placed it at the Central Railroad bridge at 8:30 a.m. Its local column reported that Wm. Williams, "a colored man," had been shot in the leg just below the knee and that Dr. Chisholm extracted the ball the same day.

Shortly after the bridge affair, the local paper reported, a white man named John Calvin was accused of moving among the new laborers "talking in a suspicious manner" at the wharf. When he ran from arrest, a wharf clerk, John M. Harden, fired at him and hit him in the chin, and some Black workers threw rocks at him as he passed. The wire copies folded this shooting into the bridge encounter, naming him "John C. Alvin" shot in the shin or "John Calvin" shot in the spine.

No further disturbance was reported that day, and by dark the scene at the bridge was described as "perfectly serene." Three officers of the colored battalion, Lieutenant Colonel Woodhouse, Major Deveaux and Adjutant Toomer, urged the strikers to avoid violence and petition for higher pay.

The Governor and the Mayor issued proclamations ordering disturbers of the peace to disperse and declaring that the laws would be enforced. The strikers' petition told the citizens they were "not in favor of any turbulence," but they later rejected the report of the arbitrators they had asked for. No arrest, inquest or legal action over the police charge appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News treated the strike as a threat to order, writing of "riotous demonstrations" and a "spirit of insubordination and disorder" among the strikers. It credited the Mayor's arrangements with having "saved many lives" at the bridge and gave no account from the wounded men.

A Savannah wire story ran on September 24 in the Knoxville Daily Chronicle and the Richmond Daily Dispatch, which listed the clash in its news summary as "a Bloody Encounter"; a one-line version reached the Owosso Times in Michigan on September 30. The Weekly Floridian's later summary spoke of a Thursday "skirmish" with "several casualties."

A different story spread in the North, where the Washington Evening Critic printed an Atlanta special under "FATAL RIOTING" saying mounted police had poured fire into the strikers. Maine papers and the Burrillville Gazette in Rhode Island repeated a "Savannah despatch" of eight killed and twelve wounded.

The Savannah Morning News and the Savannah-datelined wire report several or five wounded and no deaths. The Atlanta special and the New York dispatch reported eight killed and twelve or "dozens" wounded, without naming the bridge, the train or a date. The local report, which names a wounded man and his doctor, is the closer source.

reader.title: Savannah railroad bridge clash (1881)
bases: Police ordered a crowd of Black strikers back from a train carrying replacement laborers and charged into it, wounding five 'negroes' (A5, A6), one of whom, Wm. Williams, was shot in the leg (A1); the setting is a strike (A3, A11), but the violence reported is by police against the crowd.

The Savannah Morning News (A1, A2) and the wire story (A5, A6) agree that police and strikers clashed at the railroad bridge on the morning of September 22 with several wounded and no deaths reported, but a separate dispatch circulated in the North reported eight killed (A4, A8, A13).

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Strikers at the bridge rushed a train carrying 150 laborers to drive them off; police ordered them back and, meeting resistance, charged, wounding five negroes, none seriously.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News
accounts.gist: A 'Conflict on the Railroad Bridge' at 8:30 a.m. left 'Several Wounded', among them Wm. Williams, shot in the leg; the paper credited the Mayor's arrangements with saving many lives.

accounts.label: Atlanta special and New York dispatch
accounts.gist: Police fired on rioting stevedores; eight were killed and twelve (or 'dozens') wounded, and two policemen were wounded.

accounts.label: Weekly Floridian summary
accounts.gist: A Thursday 'skirmish' between police and 'rioters' caused 'several casualties' and dispersed the crowd for a time.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News called the strikers' actions 'riotous demonstrations' and a 'spirit of insubordination and disorder', and praised the Mayor's arrangements for saving lives at the bridge.
Knoxville and Richmond papers ran the wire under 'Trouble With Strikers' and 'The Savannah Labor Strike', presenting the police charge as a response to resistance.
Northern briefs ran the eight-killed version under 'FATAL RIOTING', 'Rioting in Savannah' and 'A Riot in Savannah'.

conflicts.note: The Savannah paper's own report (headline 'Several Wounded', a named man shot in the leg) and the Savannah-datelined wire report no deaths; the eight-killed version came from an Atlanta special and an unattributed 'Savannah despatch' relayed through Cincinnati and New York, and does not describe the bridge or the train.
The local paper names the Central Railroad; the wire names the Continental road.

record_check.dossier: The name is printed 'John C. Alvin' (Knoxville) and 'John Calvin' (Richmond, Savannah); the local paper places his shooting at the wharf 'shortly after' the bridge affair, by a wharf clerk, not in the police charge.

Calvin's wounding was a separate wharf incident per the local paper; within the bridge clash itself no white injury is reported by the local or wire accounts (the Atlanta special claims two policemen wounded).
One wounded man is named: Wm. Williams, 'a colored man', shot in the leg at the Central Railroad bridge.

info: Thursday, September 22, 1881, about 8:30 in the morning
The railroad bridge (the Central Railroad bridge, per the local paper) in Savannah, where a train brought in replacement laborers
Five 'negroes' wounded, none seriously (wire); one named in the local paper, Wm. Williams, 'a colored man', shot in the leg below the knee
Strikers were said to have rushed the train 'with the intention of driving off the hands' and to have resisted a police order to fall back
City police, 'with assistance' per the Richmond copy of the wire
None in the local paper and wire ('none seriously'); a dispatch carried in Northern papers said eight were killed
The crowd dispersed; negotiations followed; Williams had the ball extracted by Dr. Chisholm
